summary: John opens his Gospel before creation: the eternal Word, who is God and made all things, became flesh, lived among us and made the Father known.
key_insight: The prologue begins with the Word “with God” and ends with the Son “in the bosom of the Father.” Between those two pictures of closeness stands verse 14: “the Word became flesh.” The One nearest to the Father came near enough to be seen and touched.
story: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” He was with God in the beginning. All things were made through Him, and nothing that exists was made without Him. In Him was life, and that life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.
Then came “a man sent from God, whose name was John.” He came as a witness, to bear witness of the Light, so that through him all might believe. He was not that Light; he was sent to point to it.

The true Light, who gives light to every man, was coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through Him, yet the world did not know Him. “He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him.” But to all who received Him, to those who believe in His name, He gave the right to become children of God, born not of blood or of human will, but of God.
“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.”

John bore witness of Him and cried out, “This was He of whom I said, ‘He who comes after me is preferred before me, for He was before me.’ ” From His fullness all of us have received, grace for grace. The law was given through Moses, “but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.”
No one has ever seen God. “The only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, He has declared Him.”

scene.label: “In the beginning”
scene.text: John’s first words repeat the first words of Genesis (Genesis 1:1). Genesis tells what God made in the beginning; John tells who was already there, and through whom it was all made.

scene.label: “The Word”
scene.text: Jewish readers knew that God created by speaking: “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made” (Psalm 33:6). Greek thinkers used the same term, logos, for the reason that orders the world. John takes a word both could hear and gives it a face: the Word is a Person.

scene.label: “Dwelt among us”
scene.text: The Greek word means to pitch a tent. It recalls the tabernacle, the tent where God lived among Israel in the wilderness and where “the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (Exodus 40:34). The glory once hidden in a tent is now seen in a Man.

scene.label: Grace and truth
scene.text: When Moses asked to see God’s glory, he was told, “no man shall see Me, and live” (Exodus 33:20). Then the LORD passed by and proclaimed Himself “abounding in goodness and truth” (Exodus 34:6). John says the glory Moses could not see has now been seen in Jesus, “full of grace and truth.”

witnesses.john: Only John begins before creation. The other Gospels start with Abraham, with John the Baptist’s preaching or with a priest in the temple; John starts with the Word who was with God. The prologue introduces themes that run through his whole Gospel, life, light, witness, glory and believing, and it prepares for his stated purpose: “that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” (John 20:31).

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the eternal Word: God, Creator and the source of life, who became fully human without ceasing to be God. He alone has seen the Father, and He alone makes Him known.
seeing.living: John says that receiving Jesus means believing in His name, and that those who do are born of God, not by family line or human effort. If you want to know what God is like, do not start with guesses; look at Jesus, “full of grace and truth.”
seeing.ponder: If Jesus is the One who has made the Father known, where else have you been getting your picture of God?

preaching.big_idea: The eternal Word became flesh so that we could see the Father and become God’s children.
preaching.watch_for: Twice the prologue breaks off to speak of John the Baptist (1:6–8, 15), and the name Jesus Christ does not appear until verse 17. The Gospel that follows calls witness after witness to say who Jesus is.
